Skat — Rules

← Back to the table

Skat is a three-player trick-taking card game played with a 32-card deck. One player, the declarer, bids to win the auction and then plays alone against the other two, who form a temporary team of defenders. This covers the rules as implemented by this app.

1. Players & the deck

Skat is played by three active players each hand (this app seats you against two computer opponents). The deck has 32 cards: ♦ diamonds, ♥ hearts, ♠ spades and ♣ clubs, each running Ace, 10, King, Queen, Jack, 9, 8, 7.

Card point values

CardPoints
Ace11
1010
King4
Queen3
Jack2
9, 8, 70

That totals 120 points across the deck. Winning a trick means collecting the card points in it — the goal is to end up controlling enough of those 120 points, not to win the most tricks.

2. Dealing

Each of the three players gets ten cards; the remaining two cards form the skat, dealt face down to the table. Seats are named by their bidding order: forehand (leads the first trick if they become declarer), middlehand and rearhand.

3. The auction

Players bid for the right to become declarer, using a fixed ladder of numbers (18, 20, 22, 23, 24, 27, 30, 33, 35, 36, 40, 44, 45, 46, 48, 50, 54, 55, 59, 60…). A bid states only a number — it does not commit to a particular game type yet, only that the bidder believes they can make a game worth at least that much (see Scoring for how a game's value is worked out).

  • Middlehand calls first, bidding a number to forehand, who either holds (accepts, becomes the higher bidder for now) or passes.
  • Whoever survives that exchange then bids against rearhand the same way.
  • The bidding climbs the ladder one step at a time until two of the three players have passed.
  • The remaining player becomes declarer, playing alone against the other two.
  • If everyone passes without a single bid being held, the hand is a pass-out — no game is played and it is redealt.

The number reached in the auction is only a floor: the declarer must choose and announce a game whose calculated value is at least that high, or the bid is an overbid.

4. Skat, hand games & discarding

Once bidding ends, the declarer chooses one of two routes:

Pick up and discard

The declarer picks up the two skat cards, adding them to their hand (now 12 cards), then discards any two cards face down — these become the declarer's skat pile and count toward their score at the end of the hand, but are not played.

Hand game

The declarer instead leaves the skat untouched and plays with their original ten cards. This is riskier — the skat's two cards are unknown and count for the declarer either way — but it is required for certain announcements and raises the game's value (see below).

5. Game types

After deciding on the skat, the declarer announces what they will play. Each game type has a base value used in scoring.

Suit games

One suit is trumps. The four jacks are always the top trumps regardless of suit, ranking ♣ > ♠ > ♥ > ♦ among themselves; below them come the remaining cards of the trump suit in their usual order (A, 10, K, Q, 9, 8, 7). The other three suits play as plain side suits.

Trump suitBase value
♦ Diamonds9
♥ Hearts10
♠ Spades11
♣ Clubs12

Grand

Only the four jacks are trumps (in the same club–spade–heart–diamond order); every other card plays in its own suit as a side suit. Base value 24.

Null

The declarer contracts to lose every trick. There are no trumps — all four suits rank Ace (high), 10, K, Q, J, 9, 8, 7 (low) — note the jack drops back into its own suit instead of being a trump. Null has a fixed value rather than a multiplier-based one, and comes in four forms:

FormValue
Null (with discard)23
Null hand35
Null ouvert (with discard)46
Null ouvert hand59

Null games are won or lost outright — there is no matador or level scoring.

6. Playing tricks

Forehand leads to the first trick. Players must follow the suit led if they can; if a trump is led, that means playing a trump (jacks count as the trump suit). A player with none of the suit led may play any card, including a trump, to try to win the trick. Highest trump wins the trick; if no trump was played, the highest card of the suit led wins. The winner of a trick leads the next one.

After all ten tricks are played, each side counts the card points in the tricks it won. The declarer also adds the points in their skat pile (for a pick-up game) or the two skat cards, unseen, are simply added to the declarer's total (for a hand game).

7. Scoring a game

Suit and grand games: making the game

To win a suit or grand game, the declarer needs 61 or more of the 120 card points (the defenders win together if they hold the other 60+). The game's value is then:

value = base value × multiplier

The multiplier

The multiplier starts from the matador count and adds one for each of the following that applies:

  • Matadors ("mit"/"ohne" N) — the length of the unbroken run of top trumps the declarer holds or is missing, starting from the club jack. Holding the club jack counts mit (with); missing it counts ohne (without). This is always at least 1.
  • Game — always counted (+1).
  • Hand — the declarer played without picking up the skat.
  • Schneider — one side held the other to 30 points or fewer.
  • Schneider announced — declarer called it in advance on a hand game.
  • Schwarz — one side won every trick.
  • Schwarz announced — declarer called it in advance on a hand game.
  • Ouvert — declarer's hand was played face up.

The declarer must reach a game value at least as high as the number they won the auction with — see Overbidding.

Null games

No multiplier — the fixed value from the table above is scored directly. The declarer wins by losing every trick; taking even one trick loses the game.

8. Schneider, schwarz & ouvert

Schneider means holding the opponent to 30 card points or fewer (equivalently, taking 90+ yourself). Schwarz means winning every one of the ten tricks. Both can happen naturally in any suit or grand game and add a step to the multiplier when they do.

On a hand game, the declarer may additionally announce schneider, schwarz, or play ouvert (hand face up on the table for both defenders to see) before a card is played. An announcement raises the game's value further, but also raises the stakes: failing to deliver what was announced is scored as a loss.

9. Overbidding

Because the auction number is agreed before the game type is chosen, it's possible to win the bidding at a number your actual game can't reach — for example holding the bid to 30 but only being able to declare a game worth 27. This is an overbid. An overbid game is scored as a loss regardless of how the cards actually fell, and — like any lost game — is scored at the value of the (highest legal) game the declarer announced, doubled.

A lost game's penalty, in general, is:

penalty = −2 × game value

using whichever value is higher: the value the announced game would have scored if won, or the value needed to cover the bid.

This app implements the full auction, hand games, pick-up-and-discard, all game types above, schneider/schwarz/ouvert announcements, matador and level scoring, overbid detection and the doubled loss. Variants such as Ramsch, Bock rounds, Kontra/Re, Revolution and Spitze are not included — see the project's THIRD_PARTY.md for details.
